title: Silat, Arnis, a Chicago Gym
bigQuestion: When a martial art travels from a village to a school gym across the ocean, what changes and what stays the same?

story.title: Sticks on a Closet Shelf
story.kicker: A bundle of rattan sticks in a school closet leads back to the Philippines.
paragraphs: A PE teacher at a Chicago middle school opens the equipment closet. Next to the basketballs sits a bundle of rattan sticks. Each is about as long as an arm. The ends are wrapped in tape, and a label reads "arnis."

A student named Joel picks one up. His family came from Cebu, an island in the Philippines. "My uncle has sticks like this," he says. "He goes to a club on the North Side on Saturdays." The teacher tells him the sticks came with a unit a visiting instructor taught last spring.

Joel looks at the tape and the label. "In the Philippines, it is in the law," he says. "My uncle says arnis is the national martial art." The teacher looks it up on her phone. Joel is right. A law passed in 2009 named arnis the national martial art and sport of the Philippines.

Another student asks if the sticks are the same as the ones used long ago. The teacher is not sure. Rattan is a vine-like palm that grows in Southeast Asia, and it has been used for sticks for a long time. But a school unit with tape and a label is new.

Joel sets the stick back on the shelf. "So is this the real thing," he asks, "or is my uncle's club the real thing?" The teacher says it is a good question for history class. Both the club and the closet have a story.
story.think: Can a martial art be real in a school gym and also real at a family festival? Why or why not?

lessons.title: One Word, Many Arts
lessons.mainIdea: Silat is a family of martial arts practiced across the Malay world, from Indonesia and Malaysia to Brunei, Singapore, southern Thailand and the southern Philippines.
reading: *Silat* is not one single art. It is a family of many arts with shared roots. People practice it in Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore. It is also practiced in southern Thailand and the southern Philippines, where many Malay and Muslim communities live.

In Indonesia, the common name is *pencak silat*. Some teachers use pencak for the art's movement and display, and silat for its use in defense. Each region has its own styles. In West Sumatra, the Minangkabau people call their art silek. In West Java, the name Cimande comes from a village and river where a well-known style grew.

Hundreds of named silat schools exist today. Each one has its own teachers and its own line of students. Because the family is so large, historians avoid saying silat began at one place or one date. They trace many local roots instead.

words.d: a family of martial arts practiced across the Malay world of Southeast Asia
the common Indonesian name for the silat arts
a people of West Sumatra, Indonesia, whose silat is called silek

lessons.title: Silat at Weddings and Festivals
lessons.mainIdea: In many communities, silat is performed with music at weddings, festivals and ceremonies, not only practiced as self-defense.
reading: In many Malay communities, silat is part of a *wedding*. A silat performer may lead the bride and groom forward as drums play. The drums are often the gendang, a two-headed drum. Guests watch the display as a sign of respect and welcome.

Silat is also performed at harvest festivals, national holidays and the opening of important events. In these settings, the display is an *art form*, judged by its grace and its link to the music. Performers wear traditional clothing, often with a sarong or a folded headcloth.

Some silat schools grew around villages, prayer houses or family lines. Teaching often took place at night or after work. Students learned from one teacher over many years. These community roles are older than any sport rule book, and they continue today.

words.d: a marriage ceremony; in many Malay communities, silat is performed there to honor the couple
a practice valued for its beauty and meaning, not only its use
a two-headed drum played in Malay and Indonesian music, including at silat displays

check.why: The gendang is a two-headed drum played at many silat displays.

lessons.title: From IPSI to PERSILAT
lessons.mainIdea: Indonesia founded a national pencak silat body, IPSI, in 1948, and four countries founded the world body, PERSILAT, in 1980.
reading: Indonesia declared independence in 1945. The new nation wanted national symbols. In 1948, Indonesians founded *IPSI*, the Indonesian Pencak Silat Association, in the city of Surakarta. IPSI worked to bring many silat schools under one national body.

In 1980, four countries founded *PERSILAT*, the International Pencak Silat Federation, in Jakarta. The four were Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei. PERSILAT wrote shared rules so athletes from different countries could meet. Many more countries have joined since.

Shared rules made silat a *regional* sport. Pencak silat joined the Southeast Asian Games in 1987, when Jakarta hosted. National bodies choose athletes and send them to these events. Village teachers and national federations now work side by side.

words.d: the Indonesian Pencak Silat Association, founded in 1948
the International Pencak Silat Federation, founded in Jakarta in 1980
shared across a group of nearby countries

lessons.title: Match and Art Events
lessons.mainIdea: Sport pencak silat has two kinds of events: tanding, a scored match, and seni, an artistic event judged on set routines.
reading: Sport pencak silat under PERSILAT rules has two main kinds of events. The first is *tanding*, a scored match between two athletes. Athletes are grouped by sex and by weight. Judges score each round.

The second is *seni*, which means art. In seni events, athletes perform set routines, and judges score them. There are events for one person, called tunggal, for two people, called ganda, and for teams of three, called regu. Some routines are performed with traditional weapons such as a staff or a short blade.

Having both kinds of events keeps two sides of silat in the rule book. Tanding looks like other combat sports, with rounds and weight classes. Seni keeps the display side seen at festivals. Many countries send athletes to both.

words.d: the scored match event in sport pencak silat
"art"; the pencak silat events judged on set routines
the team event in seni, for three athletes

lessons.title: Asian Games and UNESCO
lessons.mainIdea: In 2018 pencak silat appeared at the Asian Games in Indonesia, and in 2019 UNESCO listed silat traditions from both Indonesia and Malaysia.
reading: The *Asian Games* are a large multi-sport event held every four years for countries across Asia. In 2018, Indonesia hosted them in Jakarta and Palembang. As host, Indonesia added pencak silat to the program. Indonesian athletes won most of the pencak silat gold medals.

UNESCO is the United Nations group for education, science and culture. It keeps a list of *intangible cultural heritage*. That means living traditions, such as music, crafts and ceremonies, rather than buildings. Countries ask UNESCO to add their traditions to the list.

In December 2019, UNESCO added two entries. One was the Traditions of Pencak Silat, from Indonesia. The other was Silat, from Malaysia. Both countries were honored in the same year. The two entries show that one family of arts can be claimed with pride by more than one nation.

words.d: a multi-sport event held every four years for countries across Asia
the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization
living traditions such as music, crafts and ceremonies, listed by UNESCO

look.title: Two Entries, One Year
look.text: UNESCO's list for December 2019 includes two lines next to each other. One reads: Traditions of Pencak Silat, Indonesia. The other reads: Silat, Malaysia. Each entry was sent in by its own country.
look.prompt: Why might UNESCO list silat twice, once for each country, instead of once for the whole region?

check.q: Which country hosted the 2018 Asian Games and added pencak silat?
check.why: Indonesia hosted the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta and Palembang and added pencak silat.

check.q: What does intangible cultural heritage mean?
choices: living traditions such as music, crafts and ceremonies
check.why: Intangible cultural heritage means living traditions, not buildings.

choices: silat traditions from both Indonesia and Malaysia
check.why: In December 2019 UNESCO listed the Traditions of Pencak Silat (Indonesia) and Silat (Malaysia).

lessons.title: Names Borrowed From Spanish
lessons.mainIdea: The Filipino stick-based arts go by several names, and two of them, arnis and eskrima, come from Spanish words.
reading: The Philippines has a family of martial arts known for sticks and blades. People call them by several names. The best known are *arnis*, *eskrima* and kali. In many clubs, the names are used almost as if they mean the same thing.

Two of these names come from Spanish. Spain ruled the Philippines from the 1500s until 1898. The word arnis likely comes from the Spanish arnés, meaning armor or harness. The word eskrima comes from the Spanish esgrima, meaning fencing.

The origin of the name kali is debated. Some teachers link it to older Filipino words. Historians say the evidence is thin. What is clear is that the arts belong to many islands and languages, such as Cebuano, Ilocano and Tagalog. Each region kept its own teachers and styles.

words.d: a Filipino martial art known for sticks and blades; the name likely comes from Spanish arnés
another name for the Filipino stick arts, from Spanish esgrima, meaning fencing
a vine-like palm of Southeast Asia, used to make arnis sticks

lessons.title: Mactan, 1521, and the Stories After
lessons.mainIdea: Lapulapu's forces defeated Ferdinand Magellan at Mactan in 1521; later claims that they used arnis are a proud story, not a documented fact.
reading: In April 1521, the Portuguese sailor Ferdinand Magellan, leading a Spanish fleet, landed on the island of Mactan. Its chief, *Lapulapu*, refused to submit. In the fight that followed, Magellan was killed. Lapulapu is honored today as a Filipino hero.

Our main record of the battle comes from Antonio *Pigafetta*. He was an Italian who sailed with Magellan and kept a journal. He wrote that the fighters of Mactan used spears, shields and blades, and that there were very many of them. He does not name any martial art.

Many arnis teachers today say that Lapulapu's fighters practiced an early form of their art. This is a proud story. Historians note that no record from 1521 names such an art. The story is best held as tradition, beside the journal as evidence.

words.d: the chief of Mactan whose forces defeated Magellan in 1521
Antonio Pigafetta, an Italian who sailed with Magellan and wrote the main account of the voyage

look.title: An Eyewitness Journal
look.text: The islanders came at us in great numbers, with spears of bamboo, shields and blades. They aimed at our legs, which had no armor, and would not stop fighting.
look.cite: Antonio Pigafetta, Report on the First Voyage Around the World (written in the 1520s)
look.prompt: What does Pigafetta tell us about the fighters of Mactan? What does he not tell us?

check.q: Who led the forces that defeated Magellan at Mactan in 1521?
check.why: Lapulapu, the chief of Mactan, led the forces that defeated Magellan.

check.q: Who wrote the main account of the battle at Mactan?
check.why: Antonio Pigafetta, who sailed with Magellan, kept the main journal of the voyage.

check.q: Why is the claim that Lapulapu's fighters used arnis treated as tradition?
choices: No record from 1521 names such an art.

check.why: No record from 1521 names arnis, so the claim is a proud tradition, not a documented fact.

lessons.title: A National Martial Art by Law
lessons.mainIdea: Republic Act No. 9850, signed in 2009, made arnis the national martial art and sport of the Philippines.
reading: In 2009, the Philippine Congress passed *Republic Act No. 9850*. President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo signed it in December of that year. The law declared arnis the *national martial art* and sport of the Philippines.

The law named the Philippine Sports Commission as the lead agency for arnis. It also called for arnis to be promoted in schools and national sports events. Since then, many Filipino schoolchildren meet arnis in physical education classes.

A national law is a strong kind of recognition. It turns a family of local arts into a symbol of the whole country. Some older teachers welcomed this. Others worried that one official version might crowd out the many island styles.

words.d: the 2009 Philippine law that made arnis the national martial art and sport
a martial art a country officially names as a symbol of the nation
the government body for sports in the Philippines

look.prompt: What is each teacher hopeful or worried about? Can both be right?

lessons.title: Arnis as a Sport
lessons.mainIdea: Sport arnis uses padded sticks, protective gear and scoring rules, and it first appeared at the Southeast Asian Games in 2005.
reading: In the later 1900s, arnis groups began to hold more scored matches. To make matches safer, groups added *protective gear*, such as padded vests and helmets with face cages. Some rules use sticks covered in foam padding. Referees and judges score each round.

Different groups wrote different rule books. The World Eskrima Kali Arnis Federation, called *WEKAF*, was founded in Cebu in the late 1980s. It holds world championships with athletes from many countries. Other groups in the Philippines keep their own rules.

Arnis first appeared at the Southeast Asian Games in 2005, when the Philippines hosted. Sport events include scored matches and events judged on set routines. Many clubs call a routine *anyo*. Like silat, arnis keeps both a match side and a display side.

words.d: padded vests, helmets and other equipment worn to make matches safer
the World Eskrima Kali Arnis Federation, founded in Cebu in the late 1980s
a set routine performed and judged in sport arnis

lessons.title: Laws That Shaped Filipino Migration
lessons.mainIdea: U.S. laws in 1903, 1934, 1946 and 1965 opened and closed the door for Filipinos coming to the United States.
reading: The United States took control of the Philippines from Spain in 1898, after the Spanish-American War. In 1903, the U.S.-run government of the islands created the *pensionado* program. It sent Filipino students to study at American colleges, including schools in the Midwest.

In the 1920s, many Filipino men came to work on farms in California and Hawaii and in cities such as Chicago. The Tydings-McDuffie Act of 1934 promised the Philippines independence. It also cut Filipino immigration to 50 people a year. The Luce-Celler Act of 1946 let Filipino immigrants become U.S. citizens. The Philippines became independent that same year.

The *Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965* ended the old quota system based on national origin. After it, many more Filipino families came to the United States. Many were nurses, doctors and engineers. They brought their arts, foods and languages with them, including arnis.

words.d: a Filipino student sent to study in the United States under a program begun in 1903
a limit on how many people from a country may immigrate each year
the U.S. law that ended immigration quotas based on national origin

lessons.title: Stockton, Chicago and Community Clubs
lessons.mainIdea: Filipino communities in Stockton, Chicago and other cities kept eskrima alive in family backyards and community clubs before it reached public classes.
reading: Stockton, California, had one of the largest Filipino communities in the United States in the early 1900s. Its downtown area was known as Little Manila. Farm workers from the Philippines taught eskrima to one another in backyards and halls. For years, many teachers taught only Filipino students.

In the 1960s, Stockton teachers began to open their classes to the public. *Angel Cabales* is often named as one of the first to run an eskrima school open to anyone. Students from many backgrounds came. Some of them later became well-known teachers themselves.

Chicago also has a long Filipino history. Pensionado students studied in the Midwest after 1903. In the 1920s and 1930s, many Filipino men in Chicago worked for the *Pullman Company*, which ran sleeping cars on the railroads. Later, many Filipino nurses came to Chicago hospitals. Community groups and clubs grew with the population, and some taught arnis.

an eskrima teacher in Stockton, California, often named as one of the first to open a school to the public

lessons.title: Gym and Festival, Both Real
lessons.mainIdea: When silat and arnis travel, they live in both sport gyms and community gatherings, and each setting is a real part of the tradition.
reading: Silat also traveled. After the Netherlands recognized Indonesia's independence in 1949, many Indo families, of mixed Dutch and Indonesian descent, moved to the Netherlands. Some brought pencak silat with them. Silat clubs grew in Dutch cities and later spread across Europe.

In a new country, an art often lives in two places. One is the sport gym, with rules, weight classes, scoring and a national federation. The other is the community gathering, where the art is shown at weddings, holidays and family events. Both places have teachers who learned from older teachers.

It can be tempting to call one version real and the other fake. Historians of the *diaspora* see it differently. A school unit, a Saturday club and a village festival are all part of the art's history. Each setting keeps some parts and changes others.

words.d: a person of mixed Dutch and Indonesian descent
people who live far from their homeland, and their communities
